name: Asbury Automotive
headline: A large car-dealer group whose franchise rights, service work and finance income are hard for rivals to copy.
what_short: Franchised car dealerships and collision centers
what_it_does: Asbury runs 171 franchised car dealerships (36 brands) and 39 collision centers in 15 states. It sells new and used cars, services them, and arranges loans and insurance-type products. It also has its own business that sells vehicle service contracts through its stores.
why_it_passed: State franchise laws mean only a franchised dealer may sell a brand new, and they limit rivals from opening a same-brand store nearby.
Parts and service plus finance and insurance make up 71% of its gross profit, and warranty and recall work must be done at a franchised dealer.
On the tangible capital it needs, it earned 16% to 31% before tax every year from 2011 to 2019, and 27.9% in 2025.
Even in the 2009 slump it still made $90.9 million from operations on $3.23 billion of revenue.
why_not_now: At $165.28 a share, the price would earn about 8.2% a year in cash with no growth, below the roughly 10% the analysis requires. The cash it produces has not covered its acquisition spending, and the analysis's central value is far below the price.
watch: The automaker-granted franchise rights could be weakened by direct sales from electric-vehicle makers.
It carries about $3.5 billion of debt plus $1.8 billion of vehicle floor-plan loans.
The Federal Trade Commission has a complaint about add-on product sales and credit law at three Texas stores, still unresolved.
Toyota and Lexus are 30% of new-vehicle revenue.
